Remember oxygen pulls electrons strongly, so O is δ- and H is δ+. A hydrogen bond must then join a δ+ H on one molecule to a δ- O on the other molecule.
walkthrough:
**Recall what water looks like**

Think of water as H-O-H. Oxygen sits in the centre, with two hydrogens attached.

So first cross out any diagram that shows O-H-O or H-H-O. Only a correct H-O-H pair can be right.

**Get the partial charges right**

Oxygen is very electronegative, so it pulls the shared electrons towards itself.

That means: O is $\delta^-$ and each H is $\delta^+$. Any diagram that labels O as $\delta^+$ or H as $\delta^-$ is wrong straight away.

**Place the hydrogen bond correctly**

A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between molecules, shown as a dashed line.

It always forms between the $\delta^+$ hydrogen of one water and the $\delta^-$ oxygen of a neighbouring water: $H^{\delta+} \cdots O^{\delta-}$. Only diagram C shows H-O-H molecules, correct charges, and this $H \cdots O$ link.

options.A: Charges are reversed, showing O as δ+ and H as δ-. In real water O is δ- and H is δ+.
options.B: Molecules are drawn as O-H-O instead of H-O-H, so they are not water molecules even though the dashed line is between O and H.
options.C: Shows two correct H-O-H molecules with O as δ- and H as δ+, and the hydrogen bond correctly joins H δ+ of one to O δ- of the other.
options.D: Molecules are O-H-O not H-O-H, and charges are mixed up with H shown as δ- and O shown as δ+.
